catalog_quote: Before turning to the main topic of the paper, adjectives, I briefly lay out the morphophonological structure of the language. Seenku has undergone extensive reduction, leaving the vocabulary largely mono- and sesquisyllabic, a term generally reserved for Southeast Asian languages (Matisoff 1990, Brunelle and Pittayaporn 2012, Butler 2014). In other words, where many other Mande languages see reduction or deletion of certain vowels in certain stress positions (e.g. initial unstressed high vowels in an iambic foot, Bambara, Green 2010), these reduction patterns in Seenku have resulted in restructuring and concurrent loss of the stress system, with the original full vowels ostensibly no longer part of the underlying representation. As seen in (1a), monosyllabic words can have either a short or long vowel, with or without a coda nasal.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Seenku is a four-level tone language (X, L, H, S plus contours); the author states that the historical vowel reductions that produced its mono- and sesquisyllabic vocabulary came with the loss of the (Mande iambic-foot) stress system, so no synchronic word-stress rule is posited — word prosody is tonal only.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the remark is a passing statement in a morphosyntax paper, and the dedicated phonetic description (JIPA 2020 Illustration) does not discuss stress at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical vocabulary); the sesquisyllabic half-syllable is not a tone-bearing unit. Data are from the Southern dialect (Bouendé/Gbeneku), author's fieldwork 2012-2016.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data (McPherson 2017, 2019, 2020 JIPA, 2021) describe the Southern dialect (Gbeneku, village of Bouendé/Gbene, ~11-12k speakers); Prost 1971 describes the Northern dialect (Timiku, Karangasso, ~5k). Glottolog 5.1 seek1238 is the language-level node and lists no dialect glottocodes (its reference records label the varieties 'Sembla of Bouendé / Southern Seeku' and 'Sembla of Karangasso / Northern Seeku').

sources.locator: §2 'Language background', paragraph 4 (OpenEdition ¶4); OpenEdition p. 2 (PDF page 3 counting the cover)
sources.note: §2 'Language background' ¶4: Seenku's vowel reduction (yielding mono-/sesquisyllabic words) 'resulted in restructuring and concurrent loss of the stress system'; other Mande languages reduce unstressed vowels in an iambic foot, Seenku no longer has that stress system. Tone is the only word prosody described (four levels).
No phonology content; cites Prost 1971 and McPherson 2017/2020 only.

sources.note: §2.1 (p. 205) gives the four-level tone system and mono-/sesquisyllabic word structure; no mention of stress or accent (the only 'accent' hit is 'acute and grave accent' diacritics).

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2020. Seenku (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(2): 220-239. doi:10.1017/S0025100318000312 (open access)
sources.note: Silent on stress/accent (zero hits in body). Describes four contrastive tone levels X/L/H/S plus contour tones, downstep/downdrift (pp. 233-237); 'Syllable and word structure' p. 228: sesquisyllabic words 'have evolved from iambic reduction of disyllabic words, still attested in other Mande languages' (diachronic, not a synchronic stress statement). Southern dialect (Bouendé).

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2019. Seenku argument-head tone sandhi: Allomorph selection in a cyclic grammar. Glossa 4(1): 22, 1-41. doi:10.5334/gjgl.798 (CC BY)
sources.note: No statement on stress. p. 4: sesquisyllabic forms are 'a case of extreme reduction of erstwhile V1 in the Mande "metrical foot" (Vydrine 2010)'; the half syllable is not a tone-bearing unit. Sandhi domains treated as phonological phrases (§5.2).
